title: News Feed
prompt: Design the home feed for a social app: when I open it, I see recent posts from the people I follow, newest or best first, and I can keep scrolling.

clarify.q: Is the feed chronological or ranked?
clarify.why: Chronological can be served straight from a precomputed list. Ranking adds a scoring step at read time over a larger candidate set, which changes how many items we must fetch per request.

clarify.q: How skewed is the follow graph? What is the largest follower count?
clarify.why: If a few accounts have tens of millions of followers, pushing every post into every follower's feed is too expensive for them. That is the single fact that forces a hybrid design.

clarify.q: How fresh must the feed be after someone I follow posts?
clarify.why: Seconds of delay lets us fan out asynchronously through a queue. Strictly immediate would push work into the read path.

clarify.q: Do we follow people only, or also groups, pages and hashtags?
clarify.why: Each new source type is another kind of edge to merge. Pages behave like celebrities: large audiences, few writers.

clarify.q: What does a feed item contain: text, images, video?
clarify.why: Media is served by a CDN and stays out of the feed store. The feed itself should hold IDs only, which keeps it small.

clarify.q: How far back can people scroll?
clarify.why: If almost nobody scrolls past a few hundred items, we only precompute that many and fall back to a slower path for the deep tail.

clarify.q: What happens on unfollow, delete or block?
clarify.why: Precomputed feeds hold stale entries. We need either cleanup on write or filtering on read.

functional: A user sees posts from accounts they follow, newest first (ranking is a follow-up layer).
Posting is visible to followers within a few seconds.
Infinite scroll with a stable cursor: no duplicates or gaps while new posts arrive.
Deleted posts and posts from unfollowed or blocked accounts do not appear.
Each item shows author, content and like/comment counts.
nonFunctional: Feed first page p99 under 200 ms server time.
Read availability 99.99%; a stale feed is acceptable, an error page is not.
New post visible to 99% of followers within 5 s; celebrity posts may take up to 30 s to reach all.
Eventual consistency is fine for counts and ordering.
outOfScope: The ranking model itself (we design where it plugs in).
Ads insertion, notifications, and post creation media upload.

assumptions: Each user opens the feed 10 times a day
150 M new posts per day (0.5 per DAU)
Average 200 followers per poster; the largest accounts have 50 M+
Precompute the newest 500 post IDs per active user, 16 bytes per entry (post id + timestamp)

steps.label: One celebrity post
steps.math: 50 M followers / 100 k inserts/s dedicated capacity = 500 s
steps.result: ≈ 8 minutes of fan-out for one post: unacceptable

steps.label: Timeline cache size
steps.math: 500 entries × 16 B = 8 KB/user; 300 M × 8 KB = 2.4 TB
steps.result: ≈ 2.4 TB in memory: ~40 Redis nodes at 64 GB, before replicas

estimates.takeaway: Reads are 20× the posts, and each read must be fast, so precomputing feeds (fan-out on write) is attractive. But the average 350 k inserts/s hides a long tail: one 50 M-follower account would need minutes of fan-out per post. So: push for normal accounts, pull for very large ones, and keep the timeline cache to IDs only so 2.4 TB is enough.

api.note: Cursor is opaque: encodes the last seen (timestamp, postId). Never offset-based.
Idempotency-Key header so a retried upload does not create two posts.
Marks deleted; feeds filter it on read and a background job removes entries.
Triggers a small backfill of the target's recent posts into the follower's feed.
Published via outbox from the post service.

entities.name: Post
entities.store: Sharded MySQL or Cassandra by postId, fronted by a cache
entities.why: Source of truth. Feed reads hydrate posts by ID in batches from a cache.

entities.name: Follow
entities.store: Sharded by followerId, plus a reverse table sharded by followeeId
entities.why: Fan-out needs 'who follows X' (reverse); feed merge needs 'whom do I follow' (forward). Two tables, two shard keys.

entities.name: HomeTimeline
entities.store: Redis sorted set per user, key feed:{userId}
entities.why: Capped at 500 entries with ZADD + ZREMRANGEBYRANK. Only IDs, so it stays small and rebuildable.

entities.name: AuthorTimeline
entities.store: Redis sorted set per author for large accounts, key posts:{authorId}
entities.why: For pull-model accounts we read their recent posts at feed time instead of pushing.

data.note: This is CQRS in practice: posts and follows are the write model, home timelines are a read model built by workers. The read model is a cache: if it is lost, rebuild it from follows and author timelines. Use time-sortable post IDs so ID order equals time order and the cursor can be a single ID.

hld.summary:
Writes go to the post service, which stores the post and publishes post.created. Fan-out workers read the follower list in pages and ZADD the post ID into each follower's home timeline in Redis, but only for authors under a follower threshold (say 100 k). Posts from bigger accounts are written only to their author timeline.

Reads go to the feed service: it reads the user's precomputed timeline, fetches the recent posts of the few large accounts they follow, merges by time (or hands the candidates to a ranker), filters deleted and blocked items, and hydrates the IDs into full posts from the post cache. Counts come from a separate counter service.

diagram.title: Hybrid fan-out: write and read paths
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  U[Poster] --> PS[Post service]
  PS --> PDB[("Post store")]
  PS --> K[["post.created topic"]]
  K --> FW[Fan-out workers]
  FW --> FG[("Follower graph")]
  FW --> HT[("Home timelines, Redis")]
  PS --> AT[("Author timelines for big accounts")]
  R[Reader] --> FS[Feed service]
  FS --> HT
  FS --> AT
  FS --> RK[Ranker]
  FS --> PC[("Post cache")]

flows.title: A normal user posts
steps: Post service writes the post and an outbox row, returns 201.
post.created is published; a fan-out worker sees followerCount 300, under the threshold.
Worker reads the 300 follower IDs from the reverse follow table.
For each follower with an active timeline in Redis, pipeline ZADD feed:{id} and trim to 500.
Followers who have not opened the app in 30 days are skipped; their feed is rebuilt on next login.

flows.title: Opening the feed
steps: Feed service reads ZREVRANGE feed:{me} 0 199 (about 200 candidates).
It looks up which accounts I follow are in the big-account set (usually under 50) and reads their last few posts from author timelines.
Merge, drop deleted, blocked or unfollowed, then rank or sort by time.
Batch-fetch the top 20 posts and counts from caches, return them with a cursor of the last item.

flows.title: Scrolling to the next page
steps: Client sends the cursor (createdAt, postId of the last item).
Feed service reads timeline entries with score below that point (ZREVRANGEBYSCORE with exclusive bound).
Same merge, filter and hydrate; if the precomputed 500 runs out, fall back to pulling from followees directly.

deepDives.title: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read
deepDives.problem: Someone has to do the work of joining 'who I follow' with 'what they posted'. Doing it at write time multiplies each post by its follower count. Doing it at read time multiplies each feed open by the number of accounts followed. With 35 k reads/s and 1.7 k posts/s, the costs land in very different places.

options.name: Fan-out on write (push)
options.how: On each post, insert the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed.
pros: Reads are one cache lookup: fastest p99
Read cost does not depend on how many accounts I follow
cons: 350 k inserts/s average; huge spikes for big accounts
Wasted work for followers who never open the app
Unfollow and delete require cleanup or read-time filtering

options.name: Fan-out on read (pull)
options.how: On each feed open, fetch the recent posts of everyone I follow and merge.
cons: Following 1 000 accounts means 1 000 lookups per open, at 35 k opens/s
p99 suffers from the slowest shard

options.name: Hybrid
options.how: Push for authors below a follower threshold; pull at read time for the few large authors a user follows.
pros: Reads stay to one timeline lookup plus a handful of author lookups
cons: Two code paths and a threshold to tune
Merging adds read latency for users who follow many large accounts

deepDives.choice: Hybrid. With a 100 k follower threshold, the fan-out cost per post is capped at 100 k inserts, and a typical user follows only a few dozen big accounts, so the read-time merge is a few dozen small reads. Also skip pushing to inactive users, which in many apps is more than half of followers. If the graph were flat (a workplace tool where nobody has more than 5 k followers), I would use pure push. If reads were rare compared with posts, pure pull.

deepDives.title: The celebrity problem in detail
deepDives.problem: A 50 M-follower account posting would cost 50 M Redis writes, about 8 minutes at 100 k/s, and it would delay every normal post queued behind it. Worse, when a celebrity's post goes viral, millions of readers hit the same post ID at once: a hot key on the read side too.

options.name: Pull for celebrities
options.how: Never fan out above the threshold; readers merge the celebrity's author timeline at read time.
pros: Write cost for a celebrity post is one insert
cons: Each read does extra lookups
Author timeline for a celebrity becomes a hot key

options.name: Push with a separate low-priority lane
options.how: Fan out celebrities on a dedicated worker pool so they do not block normal posts.
cons: Still minutes of delay and 50 M writes per post
Storage for celebrity posts copied 50 M times

options.name: Push only to active followers
options.how: Fan out the celebrity post just to followers who were online in the last few hours, pull for the rest.
pros: Cuts writes by the inactive ratio
cons: Still millions of writes
Needs an active-user index

deepDives.choice: Pull for accounts above 100 k followers, and protect the hot keys: replicate each celebrity's author timeline to every feed-service node in a local in-process cache with a 1–2 second TTL, and serve their post bodies from the same local cache. A post read 1 M times per second then costs one remote read per node per second. If product demanded that celebrity posts appear instantly and ranked like everything else, I would push only to followers active in the last hour.

diagram.title: Reading a feed that includes big accounts
diagram.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant C as Client
  participant F as Feed service
  participant H as Home timeline
  participant L as Local cache
  participant A as Author timelines
  participant P as Post cache
  C->>F: GET /v1/feed
  F->>H: top 200 pushed IDs
  F->>L: recent posts of big accounts I follow
  L-->>F: hit for hot authors
  F->>A: miss for the rest
  F->>F: merge, filter, rank
  F->>P: hydrate top 20 IDs
  F-->>C: items and nextCursor

deepDives.title: Ranking without blowing the latency budget
deepDives.problem: Ranked feeds need more candidates than they show. Scoring 20 items is cheap; scoring 1 000 with a model on every open at 35 k/s is not. The ranker must fit inside the 200 ms budget.

options.name: Rank at write time
options.how: Compute a score when fanning out and store it as the sorted-set score.
pros: Read is a plain range query
cons: Score cannot use reader context or time decay
Engagement after posting is not reflected

options.name: Two-stage ranking at read time
options.how: Take ~500 recent candidates from the timeline, apply a cheap filter/scoring pass to cut to ~100, run the heavier model on those, return 20.
pros: Uses fresh engagement and reader signals
cons: Feature fetch adds latency
Pagination is harder because rank order changes between pages

deepDives.choice: Two-stage at read time. Keep the timeline in time order as the candidate source. For pagination in a ranked feed, rank once per session and cache the ordered ID list for that session for 10 minutes; the cursor is an index into that list. That avoids duplicates when scores move. If the product were chronological only, skip the ranker and use a time cursor.

deepDives.title: Pagination and consistency while new posts arrive
deepDives.problem: New posts arrive at the top while the user scrolls down. Offset pagination (page 2 = items 21–40) shows duplicates when items shift. Deleted posts leave holes. Unfollows leave stale entries.

options.name: Offset and limit
options.how: Client asks for ?page=2&size=20 and the server skips the first 20 entries.
cons: Duplicates and skips as the list shifts
Deep offsets are slow

options.name: Cursor on (createdAt, postId)
options.how: Return the last item's key; next page asks for items strictly older.
pros: Stable under inserts at the head
cons: Opaque to the client
Ranked feeds need a session snapshot instead

deepDives.choice: Cursor. New posts above the viewport are surfaced by a separate 'new posts' pill that refetches the head. Deletes and blocks are filtered at read time using a small per-user block set and the post's deleted flag, with lazy cleanup of the timeline. On unfollow, filter at read time immediately and let a background job remove the entries.

failures: Feeds on that shard are rebuilt on demand by pulling from followees' author timelines (slower first load), rate-limited so rebuilds do not stampede the post store.
Fan-out workers fall behind after a traffic spike
Feeds are briefly stale; scale workers on topic lag; prioritise fan-out to active users first.
A celebrity post goes viral and its key gets hot
In-process caches per feed node with short TTL and request coalescing on misses.
Post store is slow during hydration
Serve from post cache; return items that hydrated and drop the rest rather than failing the page.
Ranker is down or over budget
Fall back to chronological order from the same candidates: graceful degradation.
scale: 10× users: shard timelines by userId across more Redis nodes (24 TB), and keep feeds only for users active in the last 7 days to cut that a lot.
Multi-region: home timelines live in the reader's home region; post.created is replicated to all regions and each region fans out locally.
Richer sources (groups, topics): treat each like a large author on the pull path, merged at read time.

followups.q: How do you pick the celebrity threshold?
answer: Measure fan-out cost versus read-merge cost; the threshold is where they cross.
Make it dynamic per account and hysteretic so accounts near the line do not flap.
Also consider follower activity, not just count.

followups.q: A user follows 2 000 accounts and 300 of them are big. Now what?
answer: Read-time merge of 300 author timelines is too slow.
Lower the threshold for this reader's view: precompute a merged 'big accounts' list for heavy followers periodically.
Or cap big-account candidates to the most-engaged 50 for ranking.

followups.q: How do you handle someone who has not logged in for a year?
answer: Their home timeline was never kept; on login, build it by pulling recent posts from followees.
Show a loading skeleton for the first fetch; it takes a few hundred ms.
Then they rejoin the push path.

followups.q: How do like counts stay correct and cheap?
answer: Separate counter service with sharded counters, flushed periodically to storage.
Feed reads take slightly stale counts from cache.
Exact counts are not a requirement here.

followups.q: How do you remove a post that violates policy from everyone's feeds fast?
answer: Mark deleted in the post store and cache; read-time filtering hides it on the next request.
Do not try to delete it from millions of timelines synchronously.
Background cleanup later trims stale IDs.

mistakes: Picking pure fan-out on write without asking about follower skew.
Storing full post bodies in every follower's timeline instead of IDs.
Using offset pagination for an infinite feed that changes at the head.
Precomputing timelines for all users, including the inactive majority.
Making the feed fail when ranking or counts fail, instead of degrading.

mid: Asked whether the feed is chronological or ranked
Showed reads per second and posts per second with arithmetic
Described a precomputed timeline cache holding post IDs
Used cursor pagination and explained why not offsets
senior: Compared fan-out on write and on read with cost numbers for each
Named the celebrity problem and proposed a hybrid with a threshold
Explained hydration: IDs from the timeline, bodies from a post cache
Handled deletes, unfollows and blocks with read-time filtering
Skipped fan-out to inactive users and rebuilt their feeds on login
staff: Addressed hot keys for viral posts with local caches and coalescing
Placed the ranker in a two-stage pipeline within a latency budget, with a chronological fallback
Discussed how pagination works for ranked feeds (session snapshot)
Explained multi-region fan-out and where timelines live
